analysis.one_liner: Requires courts to review financial agency rules with no deference to the agency's own interpretation.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in October 2017 and to a subcommittee two weeks later, with no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted the eight main federal agencies that regulate money and markets, including the Federal Reserve, the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the FDIC, and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. It would require judges deciding challenges to those agencies' actions to decide questions of law fresh, without deferring to the agency's reading of its own rules. It also bars courts from treating a gap or ambiguity in a law as implicit permission for the agency to make rules, which would make it harder for these agencies to defend broad regulations. The practical effect is that banks, brokerages, and other regulated firms could more easily overturn or stall the rules they challenge.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, securities firms, insurance companies, and other businesses regulated by the eight listed agencies. When a court reviews an agency's rule or enforcement action without deferring to the agency's interpretation, the challenging company's arguments carry more weight and the agency's advantage shrinks. A rule that regulators cannot defend on a fresh look is more likely to be struck down or delayed, and a company facing enforcement can litigate longer. Over time, regulators at these agencies would write narrower rules and bring fewer aggressive cases, knowing a single judge could re-read the law from scratch.

how_it_helps.text: Requires reviewing courts to decide de novo — fresh, with no deference — all relevant questions of law, including the meaning of the agencies' own rules, in cases involving the Federal Reserve, Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, CFTC, FDIC, FHFA, Comptroller of the Currency, NCUA, and SEC.

Bars courts from reading a gap or ambiguity in a statute as an implicit grant of rulemaking authority to the agency, and from relying on such gaps to defer to the agency or read its authority expansively.
Overrides any other law: the rule applies to judicial review under any provision of law, and no law may exempt an action from it unless the law specifically names this Act.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers and investors, who rely on these eight agencies to police banks, lenders, brokerages, and credit unions. Weaker or slower enforcement means more risky products reach the market, fraud victims recover less, and the CFPB's consumer complaints against lenders and debt collectors are easier to fight off in court.

drawbacks.text: Judges would no longer give weight to the specialized judgment of financial regulators, inviting more litigation against every significant rule and slowing or weakening enforcement, which delays protections against risky banking and securities practices.

The rule applies to all judicial review of these agencies' actions under any law unless a future law specifically names this Act, a broad override that reaches far beyond a single statute and could unsettle decades of settled agency practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit goes to regulated firms in the form of easier court challenges; the cost falls diffusely on the public through slower, weaker financial oversight. A fair-minded observer can note that unchallenged agency interpretations can overreach, and a court taking a fresh look can catch that. But applying that rule only to financial regulators, the eight agencies that police the most concentrated private power in the economy, tilts the balance firmly toward the firms being policed.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its regulatory reform subcommittee from October 2017 until the Congress ended, and was never brought to a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 4, 2017 by Rep. Mia Love (R-UT) and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On October 16, 2017 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial And Antitrust Law, and no further action was recorded before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The bill had one sponsor and eight cosponsors, all Republicans, and no Senate companion action is recorded in the action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and the public came out ahead, in the sense that the financial regulations these agencies enforce against banks and securities firms were not weakened by this change. Regulated financial firms lose the opportunity this bill would have given them to overturn rules more easily in court.

sides.party_line_note: All nine named supporters — the sponsor and eight cosponsors — were Republicans, and no Democrat cosponsored or took any recorded action on the bill.

industries.note: De novo review with no deference would let regulated firms challenge the Fed, SEC, CFTC, FDIC, and OCC rules and enforcement actions on more favorable terms, making it easier to strike down or delay the rules that police them. The public pays through weaker, slower oversight of banks, lenders, and markets.

industries.industry: Consumer finance companies (lenders, debt collectors, credit providers)
industries.note: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the FDIC and NCUA are on the bill's agency list, so companies the CFPB sues over lending, collection, and credit practices could argue their cases to a judge with no weight given to the agency's reading of its own rules. That makes consumer protection enforcement easier to defeat or drag out.

industries.industry: Federal financial regulators (SEC, CFPB, Federal Reserve, CFTC, FDIC, OCC, NCUA, FHFA)
industries.note: These eight agencies would lose their interpretive advantage in court and could no longer defend broad rules by pointing to gaps in statutes as delegated authority. Their enforcement would become slower, narrower, and easier to litigate against, which works against the consumers they protect.
